details:
**Death in Venice**
Mann's 1912 novella and the most common giveaway for him. The aging, disciplined writer Gustav von Aschenbach, who was given the noble "von" at age 50 for works such as a prose epic on Frederick the Great, travels to the Lido in Venice and becomes obsessed with a beautiful boy, staying on even as a cholera epidemic spreads through the city.

**Tadzio**
The beautiful Polish boy whom Aschenbach watches on the beach and follows through the streets of Venice. Aschenbach never speaks to him; he dies in his beach chair while watching Tadzio wade out into the sea.

**Overripe strawberries and the smell of disinfectant**
Key plot details from Death in Venice. Aschenbach notices the city smells of disinfectant, which officials try to explain away (blaming the sirocco) while hiding the cholera outbreak. He is secretly glad when his luggage is sent to the wrong place, giving him an excuse to return to Venice, and he catches cholera after eating overripe strawberries.

**Red-haired men, the gondolier, and the barber**
Ominous figures in Death in Venice that foreshadow Aschenbach's death: a red-haired stranger at a Munich cemetery, an old fop wearing makeup on the boat, and a red-haired street guitarist. An unlicensed gondolier assures him "I can row you well," and late in the story a barber dyes Aschenbach's hair and paints his face to make him look young.

**The Magic Mountain**
Mann's 1924 novel set at the Berghof, a tuberculosis sanatorium in Davos in the Swiss Alps. The "simple" young engineer Hans Castorp comes to visit for three weeks but stays for seven years, until the outbreak of World War I. Characters include the psychoanalyst Dr. Krokowski and the "good" and "bad" Russian tables in the dining hall.

**Clavdia Chauchat**
The Russian patient at the Berghof whom Hans Castorp falls in love with. He borrows a pencil from her at the Walpurgisnacht carnival party, because her eyes remind him of his schoolboy crush Pribislav Hippe, from whom he once borrowed a pencil; that night he sleeps with her.

**Settembrini and Naphta**
The two intellectuals who argue over Hans Castorp's mind in The Magic Mountain. Lodovico Settembrini is an Italian rationalist humanist (a student of the poet Carducci), and Leo Naphta is a Jewish-born Jesuit who argues for authority and terror. Their debates end in a duel at which Settembrini fires into the air and Naphta shoots himself.

**Joachim Ziemssen**
Hans Castorp's cousin, a soldier who has tuberculosis and is a patient at the Berghof. Castorp's visit to Joachim is what brings him to the sanatorium. Joachim later leaves to rejoin the army in the "flatlands," returns, and dies.

**Buddenbrooks**
Mann's first novel (1901), subtitled "The Decline of a Family," about a family of grain merchants in Lübeck, Mann's hometown. Tony Buddenbrook is forced to marry the swindler Grünlich and later marries the Munich hop merchant Alois Permaneder. Thomas reads Schopenhauer and dies after a botched tooth extraction, his brother Christian ends up in an asylum, and the musical, sickly last heir Hanno dies of typhoid. It was cited when Mann won the 1929 Nobel Prize.

**Doctor Faustus**
Mann's 1947 retelling of the Faust legend. Narrated by Serenus Zeitblom, it tells of the composer Adrian Leverkühn, who deliberately contracts syphilis as a pact with the devil to gain creative genius, renounces love, and invents a twelve-tone method of composition. After Arnold Schoenberg objected, Mann added a note crediting him with the system. Leverkühn's works include Apocalypsis cum figuris and The Lamentation of Doctor Faustus, which he finishes after his beloved young nephew Echo dies. His decline parallels Germany's descent into Nazism.

**Mario and the Magician**
A 1930 novella widely read as an allegory of fascism. At an Italian seaside resort, the hypnotist Cipolla humiliates audience members and makes the waiter Mario kiss him while believing he is his beloved Silvestra. Mario then shoots Cipolla dead.

**Tonio Kröger**
A 1903 novella about an artist torn between art and ordinary life. As a boy, Tonio loves his friend Hans Hansen and the blonde Ingeborg Holm, and is mocked for dancing the ladies' part in dancing class while distracted by her. Years later, at a resort in Aalsgaard, Denmark, he sees a couple resembling Hans and Ingeborg dancing.

**Confessions of Felix Krull, Confidence Man**
Mann's unfinished final comic novel about a charming con man. Felix's father kills himself after his sparkling wine company fails. Felix swaps identities with the Marquis de Venosta, sets off on a world tour, and in Lisbon seduces the wife of Professor Kuckuck.

**Joseph and His Brothers**
Mann's four-volume retelling of the Book of Genesis story of Jacob and Joseph (1933–1943), which he considered his greatest work. The volumes are The Stories of Jacob, Young Joseph, Joseph in Egypt, and Joseph the Provider.

**Tristan**
A 1903 novella set at the sanatorium Einfried. The aesthete writer Detlev Spinell seduces Gabriele Klöterjahn, the sickly wife of the businessman Anton Klöterjahn, by getting her to play Wagner's Tristan und Isolde on the piano, after which her health declines. Mann also wrote Lotte in Weimar (The Beloved Returns), in which Charlotte Kestner meets Goethe again.
